This isn't correct. There were quite a few broad gauge railroads in the North, especially the 6-foot Erie-Atlantic & Great Eastern system (stretching from the Hudson to Chicago) and several other connecting railroads. They converted to standard gauge in 1880, of their own volition, for ease of interchanging with other railroads. There were also a boat-load of narrow-guage railroads built even into the early 1900s. The Southern railroads with assorted odd-gauges were also mostly converted in the early 1880s, not during the Civil War. 

The reality is standard gauge won in the USA because the first railroads were mostly built to that gauge because they needed to import locomotives from Britain. It worked out fortuitously that 4' 8.5" was an acceptable alternative between the cheap-to-build, small right-of-way narrow gauges and the smooth riding, large loadings of broad gauges, so there was never any reason to change it and eventually all the secondary systems that used odd gauges were forced, by economic necessity, to convert.

It gets hotter and hotter the deeper you go and the air gets thicker too and the climate would heavily vary by both depth and latitude. If it evaporated naturally, the leftover salt means little to nothing will grow and any lakes will be quite salty. The Mediterranean has been [drained a few times] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinian_salinity_crisis) and it was a hellish wasteland,though that was partially due to the fact that it happened to fall in the desert belt. If it's habitable and has been drained for a long time, natural selection will take over on the flora that colonize the area. The abundance of oxygen thanks to the thicker air will mean animals can grow bigger, make it deep enough and they could grow huge. Plants too. It is also much easier to fly leading to bigger birds and bats and, given enough time, other animals too. 

Note that draining a sea could have drastic effects on the surrounding area as well. Water moderates many climates, even deserts, and draining a sea would likely make living on the windward side an interesting experience. It wouldn't necessarily cause its surroundings to turn into deserts but it could cause droughts, famine, massive wldfires, and more.
